docs.text: How to connect to a CSV file, Google Cloud Storage and Amazon S3.

docs.title: API
docs.text: See the Connections reference.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
A model is a Pydantic class that describes what a dataset is: its columns, where it lives and how it is stored. Model.objects then reads and writes the dataset as Polars DataFrames, validated against the model.

from datetime import datetime
from smallcat import Model, ModelFileFormat, ModelWriteMode

class Customer(Model):
    id: int
    name: str
    email: str | None = None
    created_at: datetime

    class Meta:
        location = "silver/customers"
        file_format = ModelFileFormat.PARQUET

A model does not say which connection it uses. That is decided when it is registered, outside the model, so the same model runs against different storage in each environment.

import polars as pl
from smallcat import Connections, registry

registry.load_connections(Connections.from_yaml("connections.yaml"))
registry.register(Customer, connection="lake")

Customer.objects.filter(pl.col("id") > 10).all()
Customer.objects.save(df, mode=ModelWriteMode.OVERWRITE)

A complete, runnable example is in Models on the local filesystem, and the connection step is explained in Connections with the ORM. For filtering with filter, where, all and lazy, see Querying models.

docs.title: Meta
docs.text:
Meta is validated when the class is defined, so a mistake fails on import and not on the first read. Unknown attributes are rejected and every problem is reported together.

Attribute Required Description location yes Path of the data, relative to the connection's base. file_format yes A ModelFileFormat: CSV, EXCEL, PARQUET or DELTA_TABLE. The string ("parquet") is accepted too. Any other value is rejected, listing the valid ones. allowed_write_modes no The write modes the model permits. By default all of them. [] makes the model read-only. validation_mode no ModelValidationMode.STRICT (default) or COERCE. See Validation. load_options no Format options applied when reading. save_options no Format options applied when writing.

load_options and save_options are the options each format already accepts in a catalog (sep, header, sheet, hive_partitioning, partition_by...) and are validated against the same schemas. They configure the file format, not permissions. For Delta tables the write mode cannot be set there: it is chosen on every save.

A Meta is inherited by subclasses. A class without a Meta is abstract and cannot be registered.

docs.title: Field types
docs.text:
The fields give the expected Polars types.

Python type Polars type int, float, str, bool, bytes Int64, Float64, String, Boolean, Binary datetime, date, time, timedelta Datetime("us"), Date, Time, Duration("us") Literal["a", "b"], Literal[1, 2] String, Int64 Enum (StrEnum, IntEnum, or any Enum whose values are all str or all int) String, Int64 (the member's value is stored) list[T] List(T) T \| None T, and the field accepts nulls

Any other type (dict, nested models, unions of several types, Decimal...) is rejected with ModelDefinitionError when the class is defined, naming the field. Columns are matched by field name; aliases are not used.

docs.title: NaN is stored as None
docs.text:
pandas hands empty cells over as NaN (an Excel sheet with blanks, for instance). A NaN given to a field that admits None (T | None) is stored as None, so you do not need a validator of your own:

class Customer(Model):
    id: int
    email: str | None = None
    score: float | None = None


Customer(id=1, email=float("nan"), score=float("nan"))
# Customer(id=1, email=None, score=None)

A field that does not admit None is never changed: a NaN in a plain float is a valid value and is kept. To keep the NaN in the nullable fields too, set nan_as_none = False on the model (it is inherited by subclasses). DataFrames are not affected: they keep Polars semantics, where empty cells are nulls and a real NaN in a float column is a valid value that all() keeps. Reading with all(as_models=True) builds instances, so there a NaN in a T | None field does become None.

docs.title: Types a file format cannot hold
docs.text:
Having a Polars type does not mean every file format can store it. time and timedelta are the two that cannot, in some formats or in all of them. This was checked by writing and reading each one in each format:

Field type parquet delta_table csv excel time yes no yes no timedelta no no no no every other type in the table above yes yes yes yes

Why they fail:

  • Parquet and timedelta. DuckDB writes the duration as an INTERVAL and Polars cannot read that back: the process aborts with a PanicException.
  • Delta Lake has no time-of-day type and no duration type.
  • CSV and Excel have no duration type, and Excel has no time-of-day type either: the value comes back as a time or as text, not as what was written.

A model that declares one of these combinations is refused when the class is defined, not when a job runs. The error names every field, says why and what to do instead:

ModelDefinitionError: Job has fields its file format cannot hold:
  - Job.took is a timedelta, which cannot be stored in delta_table: Delta Lake
    has no duration type. Store it as a number (seconds as a `float`, or
    microseconds as an `int`) and convert it in your code.

A list of those types (list[time]) is checked the same way, and so is an optional one (timedelta | None).

One exception: Parquet written by another tool

A timedelta in a Parquet file written by pyarrow or Polars is read without trouble. A read-only model (allowed_write_modes = []) may declare it over such a file, and all() and filter() work. where() does not: DuckDB gives the value back as a number.

docs.title: Registering
docs.text:
registry.load_connections(Connections.from_yaml("connections.yaml"))
registry.register(Customer, connection="lake")
  • The connection must already be loaded (see Connections), otherwise ConnectionNotLoadedError lists the names that are.
  • Registering twice raises ModelRegistrationError, unless replace=True.
  • Using a model that is not registered raises ModelNotRegisteredError, which shows the call to make.
  • smallcat.registry is the default registry, shared by the whole process.

docs.title: Restricting what a model may do, per environment
docs.text:
allowed_write_modes can be narrowed when registering, never widened. A model that is read-write in development can be made read-only in production without changing its code:

registry.register(Customer, connection="lake", allowed_write_modes=[])

Asking for a mode the model's Meta does not allow raises ModelRegistrationError.

docs.title: Tests and other registries
docs.text:
Model.objects uses the current registry. use_registry replaces it inside a block and restores the previous one on exit, even on an exception. It is kept per context, so threads and async tasks do not affect each other.

from smallcat import ModelRegistry, use_registry

test_registry = ModelRegistry()
test_registry.load_connections(Connections.from_dict(
    {"connections": {"lake": {"conn_type": "fs", "extra": {"base_path": str(tmp_path)}}}}
))
test_registry.register(Customer, connection="lake")

with use_registry(test_registry):
    Customer.objects.save(df, mode=ModelWriteMode.OVERWRITE)

docs.title: Reading
docs.text:
Model.objects reads the dataset as a Polars DataFrame or LazyFrame, or as a list of validated model instances, and filter(), where() and select() choose the rows and fields:

Customer.objects.all()                              # pl.DataFrame
Customer.objects.filter(pl.col("id") > 10).all()
Customer.objects.all(as_models=True)                # list[Customer]
Customer.objects.where(id__gt=10).all(as_models=True)

The methods, every way of filtering, the operators, lazy reads and what is refused are in Querying models.

docs.title: Writing
docs.text:
Customer.objects.save(df, mode=ModelWriteMode.OVERWRITE)
Customer.objects.save([Customer(...), Customer(...)], mode="overwrite")
Customer.objects.save(Customer(...), mode=ModelWriteMode.APPEND)

save takes a DataFrame, an instance of the model or a list of instances (a LazyFrame must be collected first). The mode is required and has no default (except in instance.save(), see Saving one instance), because it decides what happens to the data that is already there:

ModelWriteMode Effect Supported by OVERWRITE Replaces the whole dataset with the data you pass. csv, excel and parquet (a single file), and delta_table APPEND Adds the rows to what exists. delta_table only MERGE Inserts the rows whose key is new and updates the ones whose key already exists. It never deletes. delta_table only

Saving one object with OVERWRITE leaves a dataset of one row; use MERGE to upsert it by key.

docs.title: Merging by key
docs.text:
MERGE needs to know which fields identify a row. Declare them in Meta, or pass them in the call (the call wins):

class Customer(Model):
    id: int
    name: str
    email: str | None

    class Meta:
        location = "silver/customers"
        file_format = ModelFileFormat.DELTA_TABLE
        merge_keys = ["id"]                    # optional

Customer.objects.save(df, mode="merge")                         # uses Meta.merge_keys
Customer.objects.save(df, mode="merge", merge_keys=["email"])   # replaces them
  • The keys are never updated. Matching rows get every other column of the data, or only the ones in save_options.update_columns (set it in Meta.save_options). New rows are inserted whole.
  • If the table does not exist, the first merge creates it.
  • The keys must be fields of the model, without repeats, and Meta.merge_keys must not be nullable (X | None): a key has to identify a row. This is checked when the model is registered.
  • The data must not have null or repeated keys: smallcat refuses it before writing instead of letting Delta fail ambiguously. It does not deduplicate.
  • The columns of the data must already exist in the table: a merge does not change the schema.
  • merge_keys with a mode other than merge is an error, not ignored. In a catalog, merge_keys or update_columns without mode: merge is refused when the catalog is loaded, not when it first saves. A model without keys can be registered; it fails when it is saved with merge without merge_keys.
  • allowed_write_modes includes merge by default; restrict it like the other modes.
  • Rows are not deleted by a merge (deleting by predicate is a separate issue, #32).

A mode that is not a ModelWriteMode raises ValueError listing the valid ones. These cases are refused before anything is written:

Error Cause ModelWriteNotAllowedError The mode is not in allowed_write_modes, or the model is read-only. ModelUnsupportedWriteModeError The format cannot do it: APPEND or MERGE on a file, or OVERWRITE on partitioned Parquet. ModelQueryError MERGE without keys, merge_keys with another mode, or a key that is not a field of the model. ValueError The data has null or repeated merge keys, or columns the Delta table does not have. ModelRegistrationError (when registering) Meta.merge_keys or update_columns name fields that do not exist, or the keys are empty, repeated or nullable. ModelSchemaValidationError The data does not match the model. See Validation.

Partitioned Parquet cannot be overwritten

With partition_by, DuckDB only adds files and keeps the old ones, so an "overwrite" would silently leave old partitions behind (this was checked: 3 rows plus 1 gave 4). OVERWRITE is therefore refused for a Parquet model whose save_options has partition_by. Use a Delta table, or write without partition_by.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
A DataFrame is checked against the model on every read (all, as_models, lazy, where) and every write.

Check STRICT COERCE A column is missing error error A column the model does not declare error (see below) error (see below) A column's type must be the declared kind: any integer width for int, any time unit or time zone for datetime... Nothing is converted cast to the declared type A value that cannot be cast n/a error A float that would lose decimals as int (42.7) n/a error A null in a field that is not X \| None error error

validation_mode is set in Meta and applies to reads and writes alike. COERCE suits sources whose columns arrive as text, such as CSV; STRICT is the safer default for what you persist.

Unexpected columns follow Pydantic's own setting: an error by default, dropped with model_config = ConfigDict(extra="ignore"), kept with extra="allow".

All problems are reported together and never include the values, so a failed validation cannot leak data into a log:

# STRICT
ModelSchemaValidationError: Customer does not match its schema:
  - id: expected Int64, got String
  - email: column is missing
  - extra: unexpected column

# COERCE
ModelSchemaValidationError: Customer does not match its schema:
  - id: 1 value(s) cannot be cast to Int64
  - created_at: 2 value(s) cannot be cast to Datetime(time_unit='us', time_zone=None)
  - name: 1 null value(s) in a required field

The error has an issues list (column and problem) for programmatic use.

Pydantic validates values (constraints, validators) when instances are built (save([Customer(...)]), as_models()). A DataFrame is checked for columns, types and nulls only, not row by row.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
All inherit from ModelError.

Error Raised when ModelDefinitionError Meta is invalid or a field type is not supported (on defining the class). ModelRegistrationError A model without Meta, registered twice, or asking for more write modes than Meta allows. ModelNotRegisteredError A model is used before being registered. ModelQueryError filter with where, where twice, an invalid select, as_models with select... ModelWriteNotAllowedError The write mode is not permitted. ModelUnsupportedWriteModeError The format cannot write with that mode. ModelSchemaValidationError The data does not match the model.

docs.title: Models and the catalog
docs.text: Models are built on the catalog: each registered model becomes a catalog entry internally, so it reads and writes through the same datasets, options and credentials. The Catalog is still the right tool for datasets defined in YAML or an Airflow Variable without code, and it does not validate columns. A model adds typed columns and validation, and lives in code.

docs.title: API
docs.text: See the Models reference.

docs.title: Querying a catalog
docs.text:
A catalog reads a dataset by its key, with no model. This page covers what you can pass to read only the rows and columns you need, from loading the connection to the result.

If you want the fields and types of the data checked, with Django-style lookups such as amount__gte=100, use a model instead: see Querying models. Lookups need a model to be checked against, so the catalog has only SQL and Polars.

You write Language Runs on Returns load_polars(key, where=..., columns=...) SQL (DuckDB) DuckDB pl.DataFrame load_arrow(key, where=..., columns=...) SQL (DuckDB) DuckDB pyarrow.Table scan_polars(key, columns=...) then Polars Polars expressions Polars pl.LazyFrame

docs.title: From the connection to the data
1. The connection
docs.text:
Connections live in a file (or in Airflow) and are referred to by name:

# connections.yaml
connections:
  lake:
    conn_type: fs
    extra:
      base_path: /tmp/lake/

docs.title: 2. The catalog
docs.text:
Each entry says where a dataset lives, in which format, and how it is read and written. This one holds the same data in three formats:

# catalog.yaml
entries:
  orders_csv:
    file_format: csv
    connection: lake
    location: orders.csv
    load_options: {header: true}
    save_options: {header: true}
  orders_parquet:
    file_format: parquet
    connection: lake
    location: orders.parquet
  orders_delta:
    file_format: delta_table
    connection: lake
    location: orders_delta
    save_options: {mode: overwrite}

docs.title: 3. Load both and write something
docs.text:
import polars as pl
from smallcat import Connections
from smallcat.catalog import Catalog

connections = Connections.from_yaml("connections.yaml")
catalog = Catalog.from_yaml("catalog.yaml", connections=connections)

catalog.save_polars("orders_parquet", orders)   # orders is a pl.DataFrame

The examples below read six orders: ids 1 to 6, from customers ada, linus, grace, ada, alan and grace, with the columns id, customer, country, amount, coupon and placed_on.

docs.title: load_polars: the whole dataset, or part of it
where: an SQL predicate
docs.text:
where is a single boolean SQL expression (DuckDB) over the dataset's columns. The reader applies it, so on Parquet and Delta only what is needed is read.

catalog.load_polars("orders_parquet", where="country = 'US' AND amount >= 60")

shape: (2, 6)
┌─────┬──────────┬─────────┬────────┬────────┬────────────┐
│ id  ┆ customer ┆ country ┆ amount ┆ coupon ┆ placed_on  │
│ --- ┆ ---      ┆ ---     ┆ ---    ┆ ---    ┆ ---        │
│ i64 ┆ str      ┆ str     ┆ f64    ┆ str    ┆ date       │
╞═════╪══════════╪═════════╪════════╪════════╪════════════╡
│ 3   ┆ grace    ┆ US      ┆ 980.0  ┆ null   ┆ 2025-02-02 │
│ 6   ┆ grace    ┆ US      ┆ 60.0   ┆ 50%OFF ┆ 2025-03-09 │
└─────┴──────────┴─────────┴────────┴────────┴────────────┘

Because it is plain SQL, everything DuckDB accepts in a WHERE works:

where= Ids customer IN ('ada', 'alan') 1, 4, 5 customer LIKE 'g%' 3, 6 coupon LIKE '%!%%' ESCAPE '!' 6 country = 'FI' OR amount > 500 2, 3 amount BETWEEN 35.5 AND 120 1, 2, 6

docs.title: columns: read only some columns
docs.text:
catalog.load_polars(
    "orders_parquet",
    where="amount > 100",
    columns=["id", "customer", "amount"],
)

shape: (3, 3)
┌─────┬──────────┬────────┐
│ id  ┆ customer ┆ amount │
│ --- ┆ ---      ┆ ---    │
│ i64 ┆ str      ┆ f64    │
╞═════╪══════════╪════════╡
│ 1   ┆ ada      ┆ 120.0  │
│ 3   ┆ grace    ┆ 980.0  │
│ 5   ┆ alan     ┆ 240.0  │
└─────┴──────────┴────────┘

columns accepts plain column names only, not expressions.

docs.title: The same predicate on every format
docs.text:
where does not depend on the format. The three entries hold the same data and give the same rows:

predicate = "placed_on >= DATE '2025-02-01' AND coupon IS NULL"
for key in ("orders_csv", "orders_parquet", "orders_delta"):
    print(key, sorted(catalog.load_polars(key, where=predicate)["id"].to_list()))

orders_csv      [3, 5]
orders_parquet  [3, 5]
orders_delta    [3, 5]

docs.title: load_arrow: the same, as an Arrow table
docs.text:
table = catalog.load_arrow("orders_delta", where="amount > 100", columns=["id"])
# pyarrow.Table with 3 rows

docs.title: scan_polars: Polars expressions, lazily
docs.text:
scan_polars returns a pl.LazyFrame. You filter it with Polars expressions, not SQL, and nothing is read until collect().

(
    catalog.scan_polars("orders_parquet")
    .filter(pl.col("country").is_in(["ES", "UK"]) & pl.col("coupon").is_null())
    .select("id", "customer", "amount")
    .collect()
)

shape: (2, 3)
┌─────┬──────────┬────────┐
│ id  ┆ customer ┆ amount │
│ --- ┆ ---      ┆ ---    │
│ i64 ┆ str      ┆ f64    │
╞═════╪══════════╪════════╡
│ 1   ┆ ada      ┆ 120.0  │
│ 5   ┆ alan     ┆ 240.0  │
└─────┴──────────┴────────┘

On Parquet and Delta the scan is native, so the filter and the columns reach the file scan. Other formats are read in full and then wrapped.

>>> print(catalog.scan_polars("orders_delta").filter(pl.col("amount") > 100)
...       .select("customer").explain())
simple π 1/1 ["customer"]
  Parquet SCAN [.../orders_delta/part-00000-....snappy.parquet]
  PROJECT 2/6 COLUMNS
  SELECTION: col("amount") > 100.0

Anything else Polars does can follow, such as aggregating without loading the whole table first:

(
    catalog.scan_polars("orders_parquet")
    .group_by("country")
    .agg(pl.col("amount").sum().alias("revenue"))
    .sort("revenue", descending=True)
    .collect()
)

shape: (4, 2)
┌─────────┬─────────┐
│ country ┆ revenue │
│ ---     ┆ ---     │
│ str     ┆ f64     │
╞═════════╪═════════╡
│ US      ┆ 1040.0  │
│ UK      ┆ 240.0   │
│ ES      ┆ 135.0   │
│ FI      ┆ 35.5    │
└─────────┴─────────┘

docs.title: Which one to use
docs.text:
• where= when you know the condition as SQL. It works the same on CSV, Excel, Parquet and Delta.
  • scan_polars when you want Polars expressions, a lazy read, or to chain more Polars after the filter. Prefer it on large Parquet or Delta tables.
  • A model when you want the data checked against declared fields and types, or Django-style lookups: see Querying models.

docs.title: What is refused
docs.text:
where is parsed before it runs. A statement, a ;, an unbalanced comment, a subquery or anything that changes the shape of the query raises ValueError:

ValueError: Unsafe or invalid WHERE clause     # 1=1; DROP TABLE data
ValueError: Unsafe or invalid WHERE clause     # id IN (SELECT id FROM read_csv('/etc/passwd'))
ValueError: Unsafe or invalid WHERE clause     # amount >

SQL is text

The predicate is checked for shape, not for column names or types, and it is not parametrised: do not build it by pasting user input into the string. If the condition comes from a variable, use a model with lookups, which quote the values for you.

A key that is not in the catalog raises KeyError.

docs.title: The complete script
docs.text:
From the connection to every read above. It writes its files under a temporary directory, and needs nothing but smallcat-chonk.

pip install smallcat-chonk
python querying_catalog.py

# ruff: noqa: CPY001, D103, INP001, PLR2004, T201
"""Querying a catalog, from the connection to every way of reading.

Run it with ``python docs/examples/querying_catalog.py``. It writes its
connections file, its catalog and its data under a temporary directory.
"""

import tempfile
from datetime import date
from pathlib import Path

import polars as pl

from smallcat import Connections
from smallcat.catalog import Catalog

workdir = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="smallcat-catalog-"))


def title(text: str) -> None:
    print(f"\n=== {text}")


# 1. Load the connection -------------------------------------------------------
(workdir / "connections.yaml").write_text(
    f"""
connections:
  lake:
    conn_type: fs
    extra:
      base_path: {(workdir / "lake").as_posix()}
""",
)
connections = Connections.from_yaml(workdir / "connections.yaml")

# 2. Describe the datasets in a catalog -----------------------------------------
# The same data in three formats: each entry says where it lives and how it is
# read and written.
(workdir / "catalog.yaml").write_text(
    """
entries:
  orders_csv:
    file_format: csv
    connection: lake
    location: orders.csv
    load_options: {header: true}
    save_options: {header: true}
  orders_parquet:
    file_format: parquet
    connection: lake
    location: orders.parquet
  orders_delta:
    file_format: delta_table
    connection: lake
    location: orders_delta
    save_options: {mode: overwrite}
""",
)
catalog = Catalog.from_yaml(workdir / "catalog.yaml", connections=connections)

# 3. Write some data ---------------------------------------------------------------
orders = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "id": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6],
        "customer": ["ada", "linus", "grace", "ada", "alan", "grace"],
        "country": ["ES", "FI", "US", "ES", "UK", "US"],
        "amount": [120.0, 35.5, 980.0, 15.0, 240.0, 60.0],
        "coupon": [None, "WELCOME", None, "WELCOME", None, "50%OFF"],
        "placed_on": [
            date(2025, 1, 10),
            date(2025, 1, 21),
            date(2025, 2, 2),
            date(2025, 2, 14),
            date(2025, 3, 1),
            date(2025, 3, 9),
        ],
    },
)
for key in ("orders_csv", "orders_parquet", "orders_delta"):
    catalog.save_polars(key, orders)

# 4. Read everything -------------------------------------------------------------------
title("load_polars(): the whole dataset")
print(catalog.load_polars("orders_parquet").sort("id"))

# 5. where= pushes an SQL predicate down to the reader ---------------------------------
title("load_polars(where=...): SQL (DuckDB)")
print(catalog.load_polars("orders_parquet", where="country = 'US' AND amount >= 60"))

title("columns= keeps only some columns")
print(
    catalog.load_polars(
        "orders_parquet",
        where="amount > 100",
        columns=["id", "customer", "amount"],
    ).sort("id"),
)

title("the same predicate works on every format")
predicate = "placed_on >= DATE '2025-02-01' AND coupon IS NULL"
for key in ("orders_csv", "orders_parquet", "orders_delta"):
    ids = sorted(catalog.load_polars(key, where=predicate)["id"].to_list())
    print(f"{key:15}", ids)

title("text, IN, LIKE and OR are plain SQL")
for where in (
    "customer IN ('ada', 'alan')",
    "customer LIKE 'g%'",
    "coupon LIKE '%!%%' ESCAPE '!'",
    "country = 'FI' OR amount > 500",
    "amount BETWEEN 35.5 AND 120",
):
    ids = sorted(catalog.load_polars("orders_parquet", where=where)["id"].to_list())
    print(f"{where:34}", ids)

# 6. Arrow, for tools that speak Arrow -------------------------------------------------
title("load_arrow(): the same, as a pyarrow Table")
table = catalog.load_arrow("orders_delta", where="amount > 100", columns=["id"])
print(type(table).__name__, table.num_rows, "rows")

# 7. scan_polars(): Polars expressions, lazily -----------------------------------------
title("scan_polars(): filter with Polars expressions, nothing is read until collect()")
lazy = (
    catalog.scan_polars("orders_parquet")
    .filter(pl.col("country").is_in(["ES", "UK"]) & pl.col("coupon").is_null())
    .select("id", "customer", "amount")
)
print(lazy.collect())

title("scan_polars() on Parquet and Delta pushes the filter to the file scan")
print(
    catalog.scan_polars("orders_delta")
    .filter(pl.col("amount") > 100)
    .select("customer")
    .explain(),
)

title("scan_polars() then Polars: aggregate without loading everything")
print(
    catalog.scan_polars("orders_parquet")
    .group_by("country")
    .agg(pl.col("amount").sum().alias("revenue"))
    .sort("revenue", descending=True)
    .collect(),
)

# 8. What is refused -------------------------------------------------------------------
title("a where that is not a plain predicate is refused")
for where in (
    "1=1; DROP TABLE data",
    "id IN (SELECT id FROM read_csv('/etc/passwd'))",
    "amount >",
):
    try:
        catalog.load_polars("orders_parquet", where=where)
    except ValueError as error:
        print(f"ValueError: {error}")

title("an unknown key")
try:
    catalog.load_polars("nope")
except KeyError as error:
    print(f"KeyError: {error}")

docs.title: Querying models (ORM)
docs.text:
A model reads its data through Model.objects. This page covers the methods that read it (all, lazy, as_models) and the three ways of choosing which rows to read, and when to use each one:

You write Language Runs on Good for filter(pl.col("amount") > 100) Polars expressions Polars Anything Polars can express; lazy reads with pushdown on Parquet and Delta where("amount > 100") SQL (DuckDB) DuckDB Predicates you already have as SQL, OR, LIKE, BETWEEN where(amount__gt=100) Django-style lookups DuckDB Simple conditions checked against the model, with no SQL to write

The models themselves, Meta and registration are described in Models. A runnable script with every case on this page, from loading the connection to the query, is at the end.

docs.title: Setup used on this page
docs.text:
The examples query this model, registered against a connection named lake:

class Order(Model):
    id: int
    customer: str
    country: str
    amount: float
    coupon: str | None = None
    status: Literal["new", "paid", "shipped"]
    paid: bool
    placed_on: date
    placed_at: datetime

    class Meta:
        location = "sales/orders.parquet"
        file_format = ModelFileFormat.PARQUET

The data has six orders: ids 1 to 6, from customers ada, linus, grace, ada, alan and grace. The printed ids below are the ids of the rows each query returns.

docs.title: One query, whichever way you filter
docs.text:
filter(), where() and select() return a query. It is immutable (each call returns a new one) and reads nothing until you run it:

query = Order.objects.where(country="ES", amount__gte=100)

query.all()          # pl.DataFrame
query.lazy()         # pl.LazyFrame
query.all(as_models=True)   # list[Order], validated by Pydantic
query.as_models()    # the same, as a shortcut
query.select("id", "customer").all()   # only some fields

filter and where are alternatives

They run on different engines, so one query uses only one of them. Combining them, in either order, raises ModelQueryError where you write it. select() goes with either.

docs.title: The methods
docs.text: Method Returns Notes all() pl.DataFrame Columns in the model's order. With all(as_models=True) it returns list[Order] instead (see as_models()). Also available on Order.objects. lazy() pl.LazyFrame Chain more Polars after it. See Lazy reads. as_models() list[Order] Shortcut for all(as_models=True). Each row is validated by Pydantic, so field constraints apply. Cannot be combined with select(). filter(*exprs) query Polars expressions; several calls are combined with AND. where(sql=None, **lookups) query An SQL predicate (DuckDB) and/or Django-style lookups such as id__gte=10. Usable once per query. select(*fields) query Only some fields; names must be fields of the model. create_table() bool Creates the dataset empty, with the model's schema, if it does not exist. See Creating the table.

docs.title: filter: Polars expressions
docs.text:
filter() takes Polars expressions. Several calls are combined with AND.

Order.objects.filter(pl.col("amount") > 100)                       # [1, 3, 5]
Order.objects.filter(pl.col("country") == "US").filter(pl.col("amount") < 500)  # [6]
Order.objects.filter(
    pl.col("country").is_in(["ES", "UK"]) & pl.col("coupon").is_null(),
)                                                                   # [1, 5]
Order.objects.filter(pl.col("customer").str.len_chars() == 3)      # [1, 4]

On Parquet and Delta, a filtered query scanned with lazy() pushes the filter and the columns down to the storage, so only what is needed is read:

>>> print(Order.objects.filter(pl.col("amount") > 100).select("customer").lazy().explain())
simple π 1/1 ["customer"]
  Parquet SCAN [file:///.../sales/orders.parquet]
  PROJECT 2/9 COLUMNS
  SELECTION: col("amount") > 100.0

filter() takes Polars expressions only: a string raises ModelQueryError that points you to where().

docs.title: where with SQL
docs.text:
where() takes an SQL predicate (DuckDB), as the first argument or as sql=:

Order.objects.where("country = 'US' AND amount >= 60")              # [3, 6]
Order.objects.where(sql="country = 'US' AND amount >= 60")          # [3, 6]
Order.objects.where(sql="country = 'FI' OR amount > 500")           # [2, 3]

sql= is the clearer spelling when it sits next to lookups. The predicate is parsed before it runs. Statements, ;, comments left open and subqueries are refused with ValueError.

SQL is text

The SQL is not checked against the model: a typo in a column name only fails when the query runs. Do not build it by pasting user input into the string. Use lookups, which validate the field and the value, when the condition comes from a variable.

docs.title: where with lookups
docs.text:
A lookup is field=value or field__operator=value, like Django:

Order.objects.where(id=3)                    # id = 3
Order.objects.where(amount__lte=60)          # amount <= 60
Order.objects.where(country="US", paid=True) # country = 'US' AND paid

They are checked when the query is built, against the model's own fields and types. Nothing is declared per model and nothing is generated: the fields come from the model itself.

Order.objects.where(custmer="ada")
# ModelQueryError: where(): 'custmer' is not a field of Order; did you mean 'customer'? ...

docs.title: Operators
docs.text:
Operator Meaning Value you pass exact equal (the default when you write only the field) one value, or None ne not equal one value, or None lt less than one value lte less than or equal one value gt greater than one value gte greater than or equal one value in equal to any of the values a list, tuple or set (an empty one matches nothing) range between two values, both included a pair (low, high) isnull True: is null. False: is not null a bool contains the text contains the value a str startswith the text starts with the value a str endswith the text ends with the value a str 
Order.objects.where(country__ne="US")                          # [1, 2, 4, 5]
Order.objects.where(amount__lt=60)                             # [2, 4]
Order.objects.where(amount__gte=240)                           # [3, 5]
Order.objects.where(status__in=["new", "shipped"])             # [2, 3, 5]
Order.objects.where(amount__range=(35.5, 120))                 # [1, 2, 6]
Order.objects.where(coupon__isnull=True)                       # [1, 3, 5]
Order.objects.where(customer__contains="a")                    # [1, 3, 4, 5, 6]
Order.objects.where(customer__startswith="gr")                 # [3, 6]
Order.objects.where(customer__endswith="n")                    # [5]
Order.objects.where(paid=False)                                # [2, 5]
Order.objects.where(placed_on__gte=date(2025, 2, 1))           # [3, 4, 5, 6]
Order.objects.where(placed_at__lt=datetime(2025, 2, 1, 12, 0)) # [1, 2]

docs.title: Which operators each type accepts
docs.text:
Field type Operators int, float, date, datetime, time, timedelta (see the restrictions) exact, ne, lt, lte, gt, gte, in, range, isnull str, and Literal of strings exact, ne, in, contains, startswith, endswith, isnull bool exact, ne, isnull list[...], bytes isnull only

An operator the type does not take is refused when you build the query, and the message lists the ones that it does:

ModelQueryError: where(): 'gt' is not available for 'customer', a str field
(available: exact, ne, in, contains, startswith, endswith, isnull)

docs.title: Restrictions
docs.text:
• AND only. Several lookups in one call are joined with AND. There is no OR or NOT: write it with sql= (see below).
  • where is used once per query. Put every condition in the same call. A second where() raises ModelQueryError.
  • Not with filter. See the note above.
  • Values must match the field. amount="100" on a float field, id=True or id=1.5 on an int field, a datetime on a date field, and so on, raise ModelQueryError. A datetime must have no time zone.
  • NaN and infinity are refused.
  • None has two spellings. coupon=None and coupon__isnull=True mean the same, and coupon__ne=None is coupon__isnull=False. None inside in or range is refused: use isnull.
  • Nulls do not match comparisons. As in SQL, a null is neither equal to nor different from a value, so country__ne="US" does not return rows whose country is null. To include them, write sql="country IS NULL OR country <> 'US'".
  • contains, startswith and endswith match literally: % and _ in the value mean themselves, not wildcards, and they are case sensitive.
  • A field called sql. sql= is always the SQL text. Reach a field with that name as sql__exact=....
  • timedelta fields. No file format can hold one written by smallcat (see Types a file format cannot hold), so models rarely have one. The lookups exist for the read-only Parquet case, but there where() cannot read the column back: use filter() instead.

docs.title: Values are data
docs.text:
Names come from the model and values are quoted for you, so nothing you pass is interpreted as SQL:

Order.objects.where(customer="x' OR '1'='1")    # []   a quote is just a quote
Order.objects.where(coupon__contains="%")       # [6]  a literal percent sign
Order.objects.where(customer__contains="_")     # []   not "any character"

docs.title: SQL and lookups together
docs.text:
sql= and lookups can share one call. They are joined with AND, and the SQL is wrapped in its own parentheses, so an OR inside it stays inside:

Order.objects.where(sql="country = 'FI' OR amount > 500", paid=True)   # [3]

This is how you write what lookups do not cover (OR, NOT, functions) and still keep the simple conditions validated.

docs.title: The same rows, three ways
docs.text:
Order.objects.filter((pl.col("amount") >= 60) & ~pl.col("paid"))   # [5]
Order.objects.where(sql="amount >= 60 AND NOT paid")               # [5]
Order.objects.where(amount__gte=60, paid=False)                    # [5]

Choose with this in mind:

  • Lookups when the condition is simple and may come from a variable: they are validated, and cannot carry SQL.
  • SQL for OR, NOT, LIKE, BETWEEN or anything lookups lack.
  • Polars when you want the lazy read with pushdown on Parquet and Delta, or a function only Polars has. A query with where() runs its SQL straight away and wraps the result.

docs.title: Lazy reads
docs.text:
For Parquet and Delta, lazy() scans natively and what you chain after it is pushed down to the storage: only the needed columns and row groups are read (see the plan under filter). CSV and Excel are read in full and then wrapped. A query with where() runs its SQL immediately.

lazy() checks the columns and types, but two checks need data and are not made on a frame you collect yourself: nulls in required fields (use all()), and, in COERCE mode, values that cannot be cast, which fail with a Polars error when collected.

docs.title: Creating the table
docs.text:
Reading a model whose table or file has not been written yet fails (for Delta, TableNotFoundError: No files in log segment). create_table() creates it empty:

Jobs.objects.create_table()   # True: created; False: it already existed
Jobs.objects.all()            # an empty DataFrame with the model's columns
  • Delta creates the table; CSV, Parquet and Excel create the file with no rows.
  • If it exists, nothing is touched.
  • A model that allows no write mode (read-only) is not created: a UserWarning is emitted and it returns False, with no error.
  • An empty CSV or Excel file has no types: its columns are read as text. With the default strict validation that fails on read, so use validation_mode = "coerce" in Meta for those formats. Excel also needs header: True in load_options and save_options.

docs.title: What fails, and where
docs.text:
Error Cause ModelQueryError A field that does not exist, an operator the type does not take, a value of the wrong type, where() twice, filter() with where(), an empty where() ValueError The SQL is not a plain predicate (;, a subquery, ...). Raised when the query runs

Lookup errors are raised on the line that builds the query, not when it runs.

ModelQueryError: where(): 'between' is not a lookup operator (in 'amount__between'); 'amount' accepts: exact, ne, lt, lte, gt, gte, in, range, isnull
ModelQueryError: amount: a float field does not take '100' (str)
ModelQueryError: status__in: None is not allowed in the values; use status__isnull
ModelQueryError: amount__range: expects exactly 2 values, got 1
ModelQueryError: where() was already used: put every condition in one call (joined with AND)

docs.title: The complete script
docs.text:
From the connection to every query above. It writes its files under a temporary directory, and needs nothing but smallcat-chonk.

pip install smallcat-chonk
python querying_models.py

# ruff: noqa: CPY001, D101, D103, D106, DTZ001, INP001, PLR2004, PLW0108, T201
"""Querying models, from the connection to every way of filtering.

Run it with ``python docs/examples/querying_models.py``. It writes its
connections file and its data under a temporary directory.
"""

import tempfile
from datetime import UTC, date, datetime
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Literal

import polars as pl

from smallcat import Connections, Model, ModelFileFormat, ModelWriteMode, registry
from smallcat.models import ModelQuery, ModelQueryError

workdir = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="smallcat-querying-"))


def title(text: str) -> None:
    print(f"\n=== {text}")


def ids(query: ModelQuery) -> list[int]:
    """The ids a query returns, to keep the output short."""
    return sorted(query.select("id").all()["id"].to_list())


# 1. Load the connection -------------------------------------------------------
(workdir / "connections.yaml").write_text(
    f"""
connections:
  lake:
    conn_type: fs
    extra:
      base_path: {(workdir / "lake").as_posix()}
""",
)
connections = Connections.from_yaml(workdir / "connections.yaml")


# 2. Define the model and register it ---------------------------------------------
class Order(Model):
    id: int
    customer: str
    country: str
    amount: float
    coupon: str | None = None
    status: Literal["new", "paid", "shipped"]
    paid: bool
    placed_on: date
    placed_at: datetime

    class Meta:
        location = "sales/orders.parquet"
        file_format = ModelFileFormat.PARQUET


registry.load_connections(connections)
registry.register(Order, connection="lake")

# 3. Some data to query ------------------------------------------------------------
Order.objects.save(
    pl.DataFrame(
        {
            "id": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6],
            "customer": ["ada", "linus", "grace", "ada", "alan", "grace"],
            "country": ["ES", "FI", "US", "ES", "UK", "US"],
            "amount": [120.0, 35.5, 980.0, 15.0, 240.0, 60.0],
            "coupon": [None, "WELCOME", None, "WELCOME", None, "50%OFF"],
            "status": ["paid", "new", "shipped", "paid", "new", "paid"],
            "paid": [True, False, True, True, False, True],
            "placed_on": [
                date(2025, 1, 10),
                date(2025, 1, 21),
                date(2025, 2, 2),
                date(2025, 2, 14),
                date(2025, 3, 1),
                date(2025, 3, 9),
            ],
            "placed_at": [
                datetime(2025, 1, 10, 9, 30),
                datetime(2025, 1, 21, 14, 0),
                datetime(2025, 2, 2, 8, 15),
                datetime(2025, 2, 14, 17, 45),
                datetime(2025, 3, 1, 11, 0),
                datetime(2025, 3, 9, 20, 5),
            ],
        },
    ),
    mode=ModelWriteMode.OVERWRITE,
)

# 4. filter(): Polars expressions ----------------------------------------------------
title("filter(): Polars expressions")
print("amount > 100        :", ids(Order.objects.filter(pl.col("amount") > 100)))
print(
    "US and amount < 500 :",
    ids(Order.objects.filter(pl.col("country") == "US").filter(pl.col("amount") < 500)),
)
print(
    "coupon missing, ES/UK:",
    ids(
        Order.objects.filter(
            pl.col("country").is_in(["ES", "UK"]) & pl.col("coupon").is_null(),
        ),
    ),
)
print(
    "any Polars function :",
    ids(Order.objects.filter(pl.col("customer").str.len_chars() == 3)),
)

title("filter() stays lazy: the filter and the columns reach the Parquet scan")
print(Order.objects.filter(pl.col("amount") > 100).select("customer").lazy().explain())

# 5. where() with SQL ---------------------------------------------------------------
title("where(): SQL, positional or with sql=")
print("positional :", ids(Order.objects.where("country = 'US' AND amount >= 60")))
print("sql=       :", ids(Order.objects.where(sql="country = 'US' AND amount >= 60")))
print("OR is fine :", ids(Order.objects.where(sql="country = 'FI' OR amount > 500")))

# 6. where() with lookups -------------------------------------------------------------
title("where(): lookups, field or field__operator")
print("exact       :", ids(Order.objects.where(id=3)))
print("explicit    :", ids(Order.objects.where(id__exact=3)))
print("ne          :", ids(Order.objects.where(country__ne="US")))
print("lt          :", ids(Order.objects.where(amount__lt=60)))
print("lte         :", ids(Order.objects.where(amount__lte=60)))
print("gt          :", ids(Order.objects.where(amount__gt=240)))
print("gte         :", ids(Order.objects.where(amount__gte=240)))
print("in          :", ids(Order.objects.where(status__in=["new", "shipped"])))
print("range       :", ids(Order.objects.where(amount__range=(35.5, 120))))
print("isnull True :", ids(Order.objects.where(coupon__isnull=True)))
print("isnull False:", ids(Order.objects.where(coupon__isnull=False)))
print("contains    :", ids(Order.objects.where(customer__contains="a")))
print("startswith  :", ids(Order.objects.where(customer__startswith="gr")))
print("endswith    :", ids(Order.objects.where(customer__endswith="n")))
print("bool        :", ids(Order.objects.where(paid=False)))
print("date        :", ids(Order.objects.where(placed_on__gte=date(2025, 2, 1))))
print(
    "datetime    :",
    ids(Order.objects.where(placed_at__lt=datetime(2025, 2, 1, 12, 0))),
)
print(
    "date range  :",
    ids(Order.objects.where(placed_on__range=(date(2025, 2, 1), date(2025, 2, 28)))),
)

title("several lookups are joined with AND")
print(ids(Order.objects.where(country="US", paid=True, amount__lt=500)))

title("values are data: quotes, % and _ mean what they say")
print("a quote           :", ids(Order.objects.where(customer="x' OR '1'='1")))
print("a literal percent :", ids(Order.objects.where(coupon__contains="%")))
print("not a wildcard    :", ids(Order.objects.where(customer__contains="_")))

# 7. SQL and lookups in the same call --------------------------------------------------
title("sql= and lookups together are joined with AND")
query = Order.objects.where(sql="country = 'FI' OR amount > 500", paid=True)
print(ids(query), "(the OR stays inside its own parentheses)")

# 8. The same question, three ways -----------------------------------------------------
title("the same rows, written three ways")
by_polars = ids(Order.objects.filter((pl.col("amount") >= 60) & ~pl.col("paid")))
by_sql = ids(Order.objects.where(sql="amount >= 60 AND NOT paid"))
by_lookups = ids(Order.objects.where(amount__gte=60, paid=False))
print(by_polars, by_sql, by_lookups)
assert by_polars == by_sql == by_lookups

# 9. Running the query -----------------------------------------------------------------
title("where() runs like any query: all(), all(as_models=True), lazy(), select()")
query = Order.objects.where(country="ES", amount__gte=100)
print(query.select("id", "customer").all())
print([order.customer for order in query.all(as_models=True)])
print(query.lazy().collect().height, "row")

# 10. What is refused ------------------------------------------------------------------
title("a lookup that does not fit the model fails where you write it")
for build in (
    lambda: Order.objects.where(custmer="ada"),
    lambda: Order.objects.where(amount__between=(1, 2)),
    lambda: Order.objects.where(customer__gt="a"),
    lambda: Order.objects.where(amount="100"),
    lambda: Order.objects.where(status__in=[]),  # valid: matches nothing
    lambda: Order.objects.where(status__in=["new", None]),
    lambda: Order.objects.where(amount__range=(1,)),
    lambda: Order.objects.where(placed_at=datetime(2025, 1, 1, tzinfo=UTC)),
):
    try:
        print("accepted:", ids(build()))
    except ModelQueryError as error:
        print(f"{type(error).__name__}: {error}")

title("where() is used once and does not mix with filter()")
for build in (
    lambda: Order.objects.where(id=1).where(country="ES"),
    lambda: Order.objects.filter(pl.col("id") > 1).where(country="ES"),
    lambda: Order.objects.where(),
):
    try:
        build()
    except ModelQueryError as error:
        print(f"{type(error).__name__}: {error}")

docs.title: Custom managers
docs.text:
Order.objects is a ModelManager. To give a model methods of its own, subclass ModelManager and declare it as objects:

from smallcat.models import Model, ModelManager


class OrderManager(ModelManager["Order"]):
    def get_by_id(self, id: int) -> "Order | None":
        rows = self.where(id=id).all(as_models=True)
        return rows[0] if rows else None


class Order(Model):
    id: int
    objects = OrderManager()

    class Meta:
        location = "silver/orders"
        file_format = "parquet"


Order.objects.get_by_id(3)   # Order | None
Order.objects.where(id=3)    # still available
  • Without objects = ... a model uses the default ModelManager, typed for that model (list[Order]).
  • ModelManager["Order"] is optional. Without it the results are typed list[Model]; with it, list[Order]. When given, it must name the model that declares the manager, or defining the model raises ModelDefinitionError.
  • A model that inherits from Order gets the manager bound to itself.
  • objects is a reserved name: anything that is not a ModelManager (a field, a number, the manager class instead of an instance) raises ModelDefinitionError.

docs.title: Catalog and ORM
docs.text:
smallcat gives you two ways to read and write the same kind of data (CSV, Excel, Parquet and Delta tables, on a local disk, S3 or GCS). Both get their storage from Connections and refer to a connection by name. They differ in where the dataset is described.

Catalog ORM (models) A dataset is described by An entry in a YAML file, an Airflow Variable or a dict A model: a Pydantic class Where it is described Outside the code, as configuration In Python, next to the code that uses it Connection Named in the entry Named when the model is registered, never in the model Columns and types Not declared Declared, and the data is validated against them Write mode Fixed in the entry (save_options.mode) Chosen on every save call Query load_polars(..., where=...) and scan_polars Model.objects.filter(...), where, all, lazy Reference Catalog reference Models

docs.title: Using a catalog
docs.text:
Use it when you want datasets to be configuration: a pipeline names an entry and the YAML decides the format, the location and how it is written.

# catalog.yaml
entries:
  customers:
    file_format: parquet
    connection: lake
    location: silver/customers.parquet

from smallcat import Connections
from smallcat.catalog import Catalog

conns = Connections.from_yaml("connections.yaml")
catalog = Catalog.from_yaml("catalog.yaml", connections=conns)

df = catalog.load_polars("customers", where="id > 10")
catalog.save_polars("customers", df)

Next: Catalog reference, Querying a catalog and Writing with a catalog.

docs.title: Using the ORM
docs.text:
Use it when you want the shape of the data to be part of the code: reading and writing return and take DataFrames that are checked against the model.

import polars as pl
from smallcat import Connections, Model, ModelFileFormat, ModelWriteMode, registry

class Customer(Model):
    id: int
    name: str

    class Meta:
        location = "silver/customers"
        file_format = ModelFileFormat.PARQUET

registry.load_connections(Connections.from_yaml("connections.yaml"))
registry.register(Customer, connection="lake")

Customer.objects.filter(pl.col("id") > 10).all()
Customer.objects.save(df, mode=ModelWriteMode.OVERWRITE)

Next: Models, Querying models and Writing with a model.

docs.title: Which one to use
docs.text:
You want to Use Keep dataset definitions in config, outside the code Catalog Run the same job against different environments by changing a file Either: swap the connections file (and, for the ORM, the registration) Have the columns and types checked on every read and write ORM Decide the write mode in code, per call ORM Fix one way of writing per name (replace here, append there) Catalog

Both can be used in the same project: they share the connections.

docs.title: Writing with a catalog
docs.text: Save a DataFrame through a catalog entry. The mode lives in the entry (save_options.mode), so one entry means one way of writing, and the data is not validated against a model. It is the counterpart of Querying a catalog. To write through a model instead, see Writing with a model.

docs.title: The modes
docs.text:
Mode Effect on existing data Formats overwrite Replaces the whole dataset with what you write. every format append Adds the rows. delta_table ignore Writes only if the table does not exist; otherwise does nothing (see ignore). delta_table merge Inserts the rows whose key is new and updates the ones whose key exists. Never deletes. delta_table update Sets columns on the rows a predicate selects. Not a save mode: a separate method on the dataset. delta_table

CSV, Excel and single-file Parquet can only be replaced. To add or merge rows, use a Delta table.

docs.title: One entry per way of writing
docs.text:
Several entries may point at the same location with different modes:

entries:
  people_replace:
    file_format: delta_table
    connection: lake
    location: people
    save_options: {mode: overwrite}
  people_append:
    file_format: delta_table
    connection: lake
    location: people
    save_options: {mode: append}
  people_once:
    file_format: delta_table
    connection: lake
    location: people
    save_options: {mode: ignore}
  people_upsert:
    file_format: delta_table
    connection: lake
    location: people
    save_options: {mode: merge, merge_keys: [id]}
  people_upsert_city:
    file_format: delta_table
    connection: lake
    location: people
    save_options:
      mode: merge
      merge_keys: [id]
      update_columns: [city]     # on a match, only the city changes

catalog = Catalog.from_yaml("catalog.yaml", connections=connections)
catalog.save_polars("people_append", df)

docs.title: What each mode does
docs.text:
A file is always replaced; the second write leaves one row:

people_csv      [(2, 'linus', 'Helsinki')]

On a Delta table, starting from nothing and applying the modes in turn:

overwrite       [(1, 'ada', 'Madrid'), (2, 'linus', 'Oslo')]
append          [(1, 'ada', 'Madrid'), (2, 'linus', 'Oslo'), (3, 'grace', 'Boston')]
ignore          [(1, 'ada', 'Madrid'), (2, 'linus', 'Oslo'), (3, 'grace', 'Boston')]
merge           [(1, 'ada', 'Madrid'), (2, 'linus', 'Helsinki'), (3, 'grace', 'Boston'), (4, 'alan', 'London')]
merge (city)    [(1, 'ada', 'Seville'), (2, 'linus', 'Helsinki'), (3, 'grace', 'Boston'), (4, 'alan', 'London')]
  • append added 3. ignore found the table and did nothing.
  • merge updated id 2 (Oslo to Helsinki) and inserted id 4.
  • merge (city) matched id 1 and changed only the city: the name sent (IGNORED) was left out because of update_columns.

docs.title: ignore: a load that is safe to run twice
docs.text:
ignore writes only if the table does not exist. If it does, the save does nothing, and it does not fail. It is for data that must be loaded once and never overwritten: seed data, reference tables, the first load of a table that a merge keeps up to date afterwards.

entries:
  countries_seed:
    file_format: delta_table
    connection: lake
    location: countries
    save_options: {mode: ignore}

catalog.save_polars("countries_seed", seed)           # no table yet: created
catalog.save_polars("countries_seed", seed.head(1))   # it exists: nothing happens

first run       2 rows
second run      2 rows

The second call carried different data and it was dropped silently. That is the point, and the risk: ignore never tells you it skipped the write, and it does not compare the data, so a changed source is not picked up. To refresh the rows, use merge; to replace them, overwrite.

If the table... overwrite append ignore merge does not exist creates it creates it creates it creates it exists replaces it adds rows does nothing updates and inserts by key

ignore is a catalog mode only: a model has no ignore, and merge already gives a load that can be repeated without duplicates.

docs.title: Updating rows by a predicate
docs.text:
update sets columns to constant values on the rows a predicate selects. It lives on the Delta dataset, which the catalog gives you with get_dataset:

table = catalog.get_dataset("people_replace")
metrics = table.update("people", "city = 'London'", {"city": "Bristol"})
metrics["num_updated_rows"]    # 1

rows updated    1
after update    [(1, 'ada', 'Seville'), (2, 'linus', 'Helsinki'), (3, 'grace', 'Boston'), (4, 'alan', 'Bristol')]

The predicate is SQL, checked like a where (no subqueries) and required: there is no way to update every row by leaving it out. Values are Python values (str, bool, int, float, date, datetime or None), written as escaped literals, never pasted into the SQL. Naming a column the table does not have is an error.

docs.title: What is refused
docs.text:
duplicate keys  ValueError - the data has several rows with the same merge_keys ['id']: d
merge, no keys  ValidationError
  • Repeated (or null) keys in the data fail before writing: smallcat does not guess which row should win.
  • A merge entry without merge_keys, or merge_keys / update_columns without mode: merge, fails when the catalog is loaded, not on the first save.

docs.title: Which one to use
docs.text: You want to Use Replace a dataset with fresh data overwrite Add new rows, never touching old ones append (Delta) Load once, never overwrite a table that exists ignore (Delta) Keep a table in step with a source, by key merge (Delta) Change a column on some rows, whatever the data update (Delta, on the dataset) Delete rows Not available yet: #32

docs.title: The script
docs.text:
# ruff: noqa: D103, INP001, T201
"""Writing data with a catalog, from the connection to every write mode.

Run it with ``python docs/examples/writing_catalog.py``. It writes its connections
file, its catalog and its data under a temporary directory.
"""

import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import polars as pl

from smallcat import Connections
from smallcat.catalog import Catalog

workdir = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="smallcat-writing-"))


def title(text: str) -> None:
    print(f"\n=== {text}")


def rows(df: pl.DataFrame) -> list[tuple]:
    """The rows sorted by id, to keep the output short."""
    return df.sort("id").rows()


def people(*items: tuple[int, str, str]) -> pl.DataFrame:
    return pl.DataFrame(items, schema=["id", "name", "city"], orient="row")


# 1. Load the connection -------------------------------------------------------
(workdir / "connections.yaml").write_text(
    f"""
connections:
  lake:
    conn_type: fs
    extra:
      base_path: {(workdir / "lake").as_posix()}
""",
)
connections = Connections.from_yaml(workdir / "connections.yaml")

# 2. The catalog ---------------------------------------------------------------
# In a catalog the write mode is part of the entry: one entry, one way of
# writing. Several entries can point at the same location with different modes.
(workdir / "catalog.yaml").write_text(
    """
entries:
  people_csv:
    file_format: csv
    connection: lake
    location: people.csv
    load_options: {header: true}
    save_options: {header: true}
  people_replace:
    file_format: delta_table
    connection: lake
    location: people
    save_options: {mode: overwrite}
  people_append:
    file_format: delta_table
    connection: lake
    location: people
    save_options: {mode: append}
  people_once:
    file_format: delta_table
    connection: lake
    location: people
    save_options: {mode: ignore}
  countries_seed:
    file_format: delta_table
    connection: lake
    location: countries
    save_options: {mode: ignore}
  people_upsert:
    file_format: delta_table
    connection: lake
    location: people
    save_options: {mode: merge, merge_keys: [id]}
  people_upsert_city:
    file_format: delta_table
    connection: lake
    location: people
    save_options:
      mode: merge
      merge_keys: [id]
      update_columns: [city]
""",
)
catalog = Catalog.from_yaml(workdir / "catalog.yaml", connections=connections)

title("catalog: a file is always replaced")
catalog.save_polars("people_csv", people((1, "ada", "Madrid")))
catalog.save_polars("people_csv", people((2, "linus", "Helsinki")))
print("people_csv     ", rows(catalog.load_polars("people_csv")))

title("catalog: Delta modes, one after the other")
catalog.save_polars(
    "people_replace",
    people((1, "ada", "Madrid"), (2, "linus", "Oslo")),
)
print("overwrite      ", rows(catalog.load_polars("people_replace")))
catalog.save_polars("people_append", people((3, "grace", "Boston")))
print("append         ", rows(catalog.load_polars("people_append")))
catalog.save_polars("people_once", people((9, "nobody", "Nowhere")))
print("ignore         ", rows(catalog.load_polars("people_once")))
catalog.save_polars(
    "people_upsert",
    people((2, "linus", "Helsinki"), (4, "alan", "London")),
)
print("merge          ", rows(catalog.load_polars("people_upsert")))
catalog.save_polars("people_upsert_city", people((1, "IGNORED", "Seville")))
print("merge (city)   ", rows(catalog.load_polars("people_upsert_city")))

title("catalog: ignore, a load that is safe to run twice")
seed = pl.DataFrame({"code": ["ES", "FI"], "name": ["Spain", "Finland"]})
catalog.save_polars("countries_seed", seed)  # the table does not exist: created
print("first run      ", catalog.load_polars("countries_seed").height, "rows")
catalog.save_polars("countries_seed", seed.head(1))  # it exists: nothing happens
print("second run     ", catalog.load_polars("countries_seed").height, "rows")

title("catalog: update rows by a predicate")
people_table = catalog.get_dataset("people_replace")
metrics = people_table.update("people", "city = 'London'", {"city": "Bristol"})  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
print("rows updated   ", metrics["num_updated_rows"])
print("after update   ", rows(catalog.load_polars("people_replace")))

title("catalog: what is refused")
try:  # duplicated keys in the data: it would be ambiguous which row wins
    catalog.save_polars("people_upsert", people((7, "a", "x"), (7, "b", "y")))
except ValueError as e:
    print("duplicate keys ", type(e).__name__, "-", str(e).splitlines()[0][:60])
try:  # a merge entry without keys is refused when the catalog is loaded
    Catalog.from_dict(
        {
            "entries": {
                "bad": {
                    "file_format": "delta_table",
                    "connection": "lake",
                    "location": "people",
                    "save_options": {"mode": "merge"},
                },
            },
        },
        connections=connections,
    )
except ValueError as e:
    print("merge, no keys ", type(e).__name__)

docs.title: Writing with a model
docs.text: Save a DataFrame or a list of model instances through Model.objects.save. The mode is chosen on every call (there is no default; the instance.save() shortcut, below, is the exception) and the data is validated against the model before anything is written. It is the counterpart of Querying models. To write through a catalog entry instead, see Writing with a catalog.

docs.title: The modes
docs.text:
Mode Effect on existing data Formats overwrite Replaces the whole dataset with what you write. every format append Adds the rows. delta_table merge Inserts the rows whose key is new and updates the ones whose key exists. Never deletes. delta_table update Sets columns on the rows a predicate selects. Not a save mode, and not on objects yet (#36). delta_table

CSV, Excel and single-file Parquet can only be replaced. To add or merge rows, use a Delta table. A model has no ignore: merge already gives a load that can be repeated without duplicates.

docs.title: Saving
docs.text:
Declare the keys once in Meta, or pass them in the call (the call wins):

class Customer(Model):
    id: int
    name: str
    city: str

    class Meta:
        location = "customers"
        file_format = ModelFileFormat.DELTA_TABLE
        merge_keys = ["id"]

registry.register(Customer, connection="lake")

Customer.objects.save(df, mode="overwrite")
Customer.objects.save(df, mode=ModelWriteMode.APPEND)
Customer.objects.save([Customer(id=2, ...), Customer(id=4, ...)], mode="merge")
Customer.objects.save(df, mode="merge", merge_keys=["name"])

overwrite       [(1, 'ada', 'Madrid'), (2, 'linus', 'Oslo')]
append          [(1, 'ada', 'Madrid'), (2, 'linus', 'Oslo'), (3, 'grace', 'Boston')]
merge           [(1, 'ada', 'Madrid'), (2, 'linus', 'Helsinki'), (3, 'grace', 'Boston'), (4, 'alan', 'London')]
merge by name   [(1, 'ada', 'Madrid'), (2, 'linus', 'Helsinki'), (4, 'alan', 'London'), (9, 'grace', 'Austin')]

The last line matched on name, so grace was updated (her id changed from 3 to 9) instead of inserted again.

docs.title: Saving one instance
docs.text:
An instance can save itself:

Customer(id=1, name="ada").save()                        # merge by Meta.merge_keys
Customer(id=1, name="ada").save(merge_keys=["name"])     # keys of the call
Customer(id=1, name="ada").save(mode="overwrite")        # explicit: replaces the dataset

instance.save() is type(instance).objects.save(instance, mode="merge"): the row is inserted if its key is new and updates the stored row otherwise. It is the only place where the mode has a default, and it is merge.

  • Only Delta tables can merge. On CSV, Parquet or Excel the default mode raises ModelUnsupportedWriteModeError and nothing is written; to replace the file with that one row, ask for mode="overwrite" explicitly.
  • A model with no Meta.merge_keys (and no merge_keys=) raises ModelQueryError.
  • Every column is written: a field left at its default overwrites the stored value.
  • Each call is one write (one Delta commit). To save many rows use Customer.objects.save([...], mode=...).
  • save is a reserved name: a model cannot have a field called save.

docs.title: Updating rows
docs.text:
There is no update on objects yet (#36). Use the Delta dataset of the model's entry; its path is the model's Meta.location:

table = registry.entry_for(Customer).build_dataset()
table.update("customers", "city = 'London'", {"city": "Bristol"})

rows updated    1
after update    [(1, 'ada', 'Madrid'), (2, 'linus', 'Helsinki'), (4, 'alan', 'Bristol'), (9, 'grace', 'Austin')]

This writes straight to the table, without validating against the model.

docs.title: Files can only be replaced
docs.text: overwrite       [(2, 'linus', 'Oslo')]

docs.title: What is refused, before anything is written
docs.text:
no mode         TypeError
append a file   ModelUnsupportedWriteModeError
merge a file    ModelUnsupportedWriteModeError
keys, no merge  ModelQueryError
key not a field ModelQueryError
wrong columns   ModelSchemaValidationError
Case Why no mode mode is required: it decides what happens to the existing data. append / merge a file Only Delta tables can. keys, no merge merge_keys only applies to mode="merge"; it is not ignored. key not a field The keys must be fields of the model. wrong columns The data does not match the model (Validation).

docs.title: A registration can take modes away
docs.text:
registry.register(Customer, connection="lake", allowed_write_modes=["merge"], replace=True)
Customer.objects.save(df, mode="overwrite")

overwrite       ModelWriteNotAllowedError - Customer does not allow 'overwrite' (allowed: ['merge'])
still the same  [(1, 'ada', 'Madrid'), (2, 'linus', 'Helsinki'), (4, 'alan', 'Bristol'), (9, 'grace', 'Austin')]

A registration can only restrict what the model's Meta allows, never widen it. Use it to give a production job merge only, so it cannot replace the table.

docs.title: Which one to use
docs.text: You want to Use Replace a dataset with fresh data overwrite Add new rows, never touching old ones append (Delta) Keep a table in step with a source, by key merge (Delta) Change a column on some rows, whatever the data update on the model's Delta dataset (#36 tracks exposing it) Delete rows Not available yet: #32

docs.title: The script
docs.text:
# ruff: noqa: D101, D103, D106, INP001, RUF012, T201
"""Writing data with a model, from the connection to every write mode.

Run it with ``python docs/examples/writing_models.py``. It writes its connections
file and its data under a temporary directory.
"""

import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import polars as pl

from smallcat import Connections, Model, ModelFileFormat, ModelWriteMode, registry
from smallcat.models import ModelWriteNotAllowedError

workdir = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="smallcat-writing-"))


def title(text: str) -> None:
    print(f"\n=== {text}")


def rows(df: pl.DataFrame) -> list[tuple]:
    """The rows sorted by id, to keep the output short."""
    return df.sort("id").rows()


def people(*items: tuple[int, str, str]) -> pl.DataFrame:
    return pl.DataFrame(items, schema=["id", "name", "city"], orient="row")


# 1. Load the connection -------------------------------------------------------
(workdir / "connections.yaml").write_text(
    f"""
connections:
  lake:
    conn_type: fs
    extra:
      base_path: {(workdir / "lake").as_posix()}
""",
)
connections = Connections.from_yaml(workdir / "connections.yaml")
registry.load_connections(connections)

# 2. The models ----------------------------------------------------------------


class Customer(Model):
    id: int
    name: str
    city: str

    class Meta:
        location = "customers"
        file_format = ModelFileFormat.DELTA_TABLE
        merge_keys = ["id"]


class Archive(Model):
    id: int
    name: str
    city: str

    class Meta:
        location = "archive.parquet"
        file_format = ModelFileFormat.PARQUET


registry.register(Customer, connection="lake")
registry.register(Archive, connection="lake")

# With a model the mode is chosen on each call, and the data is validated first.
title("models: one mode per call")
Customer.objects.save(
    people((1, "ada", "Madrid"), (2, "linus", "Oslo")),
    mode="overwrite",
)
print("overwrite      ", rows(Customer.objects.all()))
Customer.objects.save(people((3, "grace", "Boston")), mode=ModelWriteMode.APPEND)
print("append         ", rows(Customer.objects.all()))
Customer.objects.save(
    [
        Customer(id=2, name="linus", city="Helsinki"),
        Customer(id=4, name="alan", city="London"),
    ],
    mode="merge",
)
print("merge          ", rows(Customer.objects.all()))
Customer.objects.save(people((9, "grace", "Austin")), mode="merge", merge_keys=["name"])
print("merge by name  ", rows(Customer.objects.all()))

title("models: update rows by a predicate")
customers_table = registry.entry_for(Customer).build_dataset()
metrics = customers_table.update("customers", "city = 'London'", {"city": "Bristol"})  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
print("rows updated   ", metrics["num_updated_rows"])
print("after update   ", rows(Customer.objects.all()))

title("models: a file is only ever replaced")
Archive.objects.save(people((1, "ada", "Madrid")), mode="overwrite")
Archive.objects.save(people((2, "linus", "Oslo")), mode="overwrite")
print("overwrite      ", rows(Archive.objects.all()))

title("models: what is refused, before anything is written")
attempts = {
    "no mode": lambda: Customer.objects.save(people((5, "x", "y"))),  # type: ignore[call-arg]
    "append a file": lambda: Archive.objects.save(people((5, "x", "y")), mode="append"),
    "merge a file": lambda: Archive.objects.save(
        people((5, "x", "y")),
        mode="merge",
        merge_keys=["id"],
    ),
    "keys, no merge": lambda: Customer.objects.save(
        people((5, "x", "y")),
        mode="append",
        merge_keys=["id"],
    ),
    "key not a field": lambda: Customer.objects.save(
        people((5, "x", "y")),
        mode="merge",
        merge_keys=["nope"],
    ),
    "wrong columns": lambda: Customer.objects.save(
        pl.DataFrame({"id": [5]}),
        mode="append",
    ),
}
for label, attempt in attempts.items():
    try:
        attempt()
    except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001
        print(f"{label:15}", type(e).__name__)

title("models: a registration can take modes away")
registry.register(
    Customer,
    connection="lake",
    allowed_write_modes=["merge"],
    replace=True,
)
try:
    Customer.objects.save(people((5, "x", "y")), mode="overwrite")
except ModelWriteNotAllowedError as e:
    print("overwrite      ", type(e).__name__, "-", e)
print("still the same ", rows(Customer.objects.all()))

The catalog maps user-defined keys to concrete dataset entries (e.g., CSV or Excel). It can be constructed from an in-memory dictionary, an Airflow Variable (JSON), or a YAML file.

The names are checked when the catalog is loaded. Without connections=, a name is resolved through Airflow on first use, as before. Inline connections (a mapping instead of a name) are deprecated because they put credentials in the catalog.
